title: Formal Verification of Continuous-Variable Quantum Programs
abstract: We provide a formal framework for Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC). While CQC is supported by photonic quantum hardware, we are not aware of a formal semantics for continuous-variable quantum programs nor of a unary Hoare logic for their verification. There are several technical obstacles to extending to CQC any of the formal frameworks available for Discrete-Variable Quantum Computing (DQC). Most importantly, continuous-variable quantum programs act on {\em infinite-dimensional} Hilbert spaces; their measurement outcomes are often {\em unbounded} and have expected values that are defined by an improper integral (or an infinite series), which may not converge. We overcome these challenges to give a formal semantics to a universal programming language for CQC and to provide the first Hoare logic for CQC. The assertions of our logic are built from polynomials over canonical observables. Besides proving relative completeness, we implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator for CQC based on our logic. Our tool has successfully verified CQC algorithms from textbooks and calculated their approximation errors for physically realizable implementations, proved the correctness (i.e., equivalence) of gate decompositions for CQC hardware, and computed the resource requirements (i.e., number of photon-number states) for achieving a desired accuracy in the classical simulation of continuous-variable quantum programs.
summary: This paper introduces a novel formal semantics and the first Hoare logic specifically designed for Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC). By restricting state spaces and using polynomial assertions, the authors overcome mathematical obstacles related to infinite dimensions. The resulting tool allows rigorous verification of CQC algorithms and quantifies the resources needed for classical simulation.
main_problem: The primary goal is to establish a formal semantics and develop the first Hoare logic for Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC). This addresses the technical challenges posed by infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and unbounded measurement outcomes inherent to CQC.
main_result: The authors successfully provide a sound and relatively complete Hoare logic for CQC, along with a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator. This tool has been shown to verify textbook CQC algorithms and compute resource requirements for classical simulation.
method: They overcome technical hurdles by restricting the state space to the Schwartz subspace and basing assertions on finite polynomials over canonical observables (position and momentum). The logic interprets implication as the subset relation on sets of quantum states.
model_or_system: The model is Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC), which operates on qumodes described by infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Key components include canonical observables ($X, P$) and the use of Schwartz density operators to ensure convergence for expected values.
key_observables: Canonical observables ($\hat{b}_X, \hat{b}_P$), polynomial assertions built from these observables, and the number operator ($\hat{N}_{q0}$).
important_parameters: The accuracy of classical simulation is bounded using the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality, which determines the required truncation dimension based on desired error bounds.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that CQC programs are straight-line (no loops or conditionals) and restricts analysis to states within the Schwartz subspace to ensure mathematical tractability.
figures_summary: Figure 11 illustrates the weakest precondition derived for the number operator under various single-mode instructions, alongside the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality used to bound simulation accuracy. Table 1 lists verified gate decompositions.
paper_structure: The paper develops a formal semantics by defining the logic's components (state space restriction, assertion language) and then implements a symbolic calculator to derive weakest preconditions for various CQC operations, culminating in verification examples and resource estimation.
why_interesting: This work provides the necessary mathematical rigor—a verifiable programming model—for advancing quantum computation theory beyond discrete qubits into continuous variable systems relevant for modern photonic hardware.
